372.title: Only a messenger
372.hook: Muhammad is only a messenger; messengers passed before him (3:144)
372.howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet as the final messenger while holding that he was a mortal man; 3:144 and Abu Bakr's words at his death are often recalled when teaching that faith rests on God, not on any person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nudawiluha, the days take turns after Uhud, and your line, days turn.

In the chaos at Uhud, someone shouted that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had been killed. He hadn't; he was wounded, and his companions closed around him. But the rumor ran through the army faster than the truth. Some men put down their swords and sat. Some started thinking about running. If he was gone, what was left? The commentators say a verse came down about that moment. And years later, on the day he really did die, someone stood up and read it aloud.
screen: `A RUMOR AT UHUD.` → `IF HE WAS GONE, WHAT WAS LEFT?` → `READ ALOUD YEARS LATER.`

segments.voice: The verse is 3:144. In Pickthall's words: "Muhammad is but a messenger, messengers (the like of whom) have passed away before him." Then it asks: if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels? Whoever turns back doesn't harm God at all. A startling verse to find in scripture: a plain statement that the Prophet is mortal, and that faith isn't meant to hang on one human life. Now the second scene. Medina, years later. The Prophet has died in the room of his wife A'ishah. Umar, a companion known for his strength, can't accept it; he stands in the mosque insisting it isn't true. Then Abu Bakr arrives, the Prophet's close friend and companion. He goes in, uncovers the Prophet's face, and kisses him. Then he comes out to the crowd. According to the account in Sahih al-Bukhari, he says: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; and whoever worships God, God is alive and does not die. And he recites 3:144. The report says it was as if people had never heard the verse before, and then everyone was reciting it. Umar said his legs gave way when he heard it. A hadith in Bukhari ties faith to loving the Prophet more than one's own parent and child. And still the Qur'an itself says he was a man, a messenger, one in a long line. What he brought, the prayer, the Qur'an, the way of living, is meant to keep going after him.
screen: `A RUMOR IN THE BATTLE` · `MUHAMMAD IS BUT A MESSENGER` · `ABU BAKR AT THE DOOR` · `GOD IS ALIVE AND DOES NOT DIE` · then, large: `THE MESSAGE OUTLIVES THE MESSENGER.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who taught you something that mattered and is no longer in your life: a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who moved away, someone who died. Instead of dwelling on the loss, ask what of theirs is still alive in you, a habit, a phrase, a way of treating people, and name it. If you pray, you can ask mercy for them.
Abu Bakr. The companion who, on the day the Prophet died, recited 3:144 and said: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died.
Your line: the message outlives the messenger. God is alive and does not die, Abu Bakr told the crowd. Until tomorrow.

373.title: Had you been harsh
373.hook: by Allah's mercy he was gentle; had he been harsh they'd have left, so consult them (3:159)
373.howItsDone: Muslims treat shura, consultation, as a principle for families, mosques and communities; mosque committees, family decisions and Islamic political thought all draw on 3:159 and 42:38, with differing views on how binding consultation is.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Bakr and 3:144, Muhammad is but a messenger. Your line was the message outlives the messenger.

Before Uhud, the Prophet ﷺ held a meeting. Should they stay inside Medina and defend the streets, or march out to meet the army in the open? He leaned toward staying. Many of the younger men, eager to fight, wanted to go out. He listened, and he went out with them. And you know how it ended. The advice you might expect next: stop asking them. You know better. The Qur'an says the opposite.
screen: `A MEETING BEFORE UHUD.` → `HE LISTENED, AND WENT OUT.` → `THE EXPECTED ADVICE: STOP ASKING.`

segments.voice: Here's 3:159 in Pickthall's words: "It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee." Then: so pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult with them in the affair. And when you've decided, put your trust in God. Look at the order. First, gentleness is called a mercy from God, not a weakness. Second, the people around the Prophet would have scattered if he'd been harsh; the verse says so plainly, about the Prophet himself. Third, right after a decision made by consultation went badly, the command is: keep consulting. The word is shawirhum, consult them, from the same root as shura, consultation. The forty-second surah is called ash-Shura, and 42:38 describes believers as people whose affairs are settled by counsel among themselves. Scholars have long debated how binding consultation is on a leader, and what form it takes, from a ruler's council to a family deciding where to live. But the core is simple. Ask the people affected. Listen. Then decide, and trust God with the outcome, without second-guessing forever. One more detail. The Prophet, Muslims believe, received revelation; if anyone could have skipped the meeting, it was him. Yet at Hudaybiyyah, Sahih al-Bukhari reports, when his companions hesitated, he took the advice of his wife Umm Salamah, and it worked.
screen: `GENTLENESS IS A MERCY` · `HARSHNESS SCATTERS PEOPLE` · `SHAWIRHUM: CONSULT THEM, STILL` · `DECIDE, THEN TRUST GOD` · then, large: `HAD YOU BEEN HARSH, THEY WOULD HAVE LEFT.`

segments.voice: Think of a decision in front of you that touches someone else, at home, at work, in the family, and picture the person it affects most. Ask yourself honestly whether you've asked them, then imagine the conversation, and yourself listening gently, not waiting for your turn to speak.
Shura. Consultation, deciding together by counsel. From 3:159, consult them in the affair, and from the surah named after it. Today's word.
Your line: gentle, and consult. In this verse, gentleness is a mercy, not a weakness. That's day three hundred seventy-three.

fork.reveal: pardon, forgiveness, and more consultation. then, once decided, trust in God.

what a scholar hears: the command came after Uhud, where consultation had gone badly; and a long debate over whether shura binds the leader or only informs him.

374.title: Every soul tastes death
374.hook: every soul shall taste death, and the world is the enjoyment of delusion (3:185)
374.howItsDone: Muslims recite 'every soul will taste death' at funerals, in condolences and in sermons, and it is sometimes carved on gravestones; remembering death is encouraged as a way to live with purpose, not in fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shura, consultation, and a gentleness the Qur'an calls a mercy. Your line was gentle, and consult.

A phone buzzes with bad news: a friend's grandfather has died. In the family chat come prayers for mercy, and then one line in Arabic. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt. Every soul will taste death. To an outsider it can sound blunt, even cold, to send to a grieving family. To the people sending it, it's said gently: this road is everyone's road, and he did not walk it alone.
screen: `BAD NEWS IN THE FAMILY CHAT.` → `ONE LINE IN ARABIC.` → `EVERYONE'S ROAD.`

segments.voice: Al 'Imran 185, in Pickthall's words, begins: "Every soul will taste of death." The same sentence appears in 21:35 and 29:57 as well; it's a line the Qur'an returns to. Notice the verb. Not every soul will die, but every soul will taste death. Dha'iqa, from dhaqa, to taste. Tasting is personal: nobody can taste something for you. And a taste is brief; it isn't the whole meal. Some readers hear a quiet hint in that: death is something the soul goes through, not where it ends. The verse goes on: you'll be paid in full on the Day of Resurrection, and whoever is drawn away from the Fire and brought into the Garden has truly won. It ends, again in Pickthall's words: "The life of this world is but comfort of illusion." The Arabic is mata' al-ghurur. Mata' is provision, things you use for a while, like supplies for a trip. Ghurur is deception, the kind that flatters you into forgetting. The world isn't called evil here. It's called useful, and easy to be fooled by. A hadith in Tirmidhi tells people to remember often the destroyer of pleasures, meaning death. Another, in Bukhari, says: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. The point isn't gloom. Travelers enjoy the road. They just don't forget where they're going.
screen: `THE SAME LINE, THREE TIMES` · `TASTE: PERSONAL, AND PASSING` · `MATA': SUPPLIES FOR A TRIP` · `A STRANGER, OR A TRAVELER` · then, large: `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle; if you're grieving right now, just breathe and skip ahead. Otherwise, sit comfortably and think, calmly, like a traveler checking the ticket, that your life has an end whose date you don't know. Then ask: if this were a trip, what am I carrying that I won't need, and what am I forgetting to pack?
Dha'iqa, tasting: brief, and personal, not the whole meal. Kullu nafsin dha'iqatul mawt, from 3:185, and twice more in the Qur'an. Today's word.
Your line: every soul tastes it. Nobody walks this road alone, not even for a moment. Go gently today.

375.title: Standing, sitting, lying down
375.hook: those who remember Allah in every posture and reflect on creation: You did not make this in vain (3:190–191)
375.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite the last verses of Al 'Imran (3:190–200) when they wake for the night prayer, following the Prophet's practice reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, and remember God in whatever posture they're in throughout the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dha'iqa, every soul will taste death, and the world as provision for a journey. Your line was every soul tastes it.

A boy named Ibn Abbas, the Prophet's young cousin, once spent the night at the house of his aunt Maymunah, one of the Prophet's wives. He had come, the reports say, to see how the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night. In the last part of the night, he saw him get up, look at the sky, and begin to recite. Bukhari records what he recited: the last verses of Al 'Imran. Today the surah ends with them, under the same sky.
screen: `A BOY AWAKE AT NIGHT.` → `THE PROPHET LOOKS AT THE SKY.` → `THE LAST VERSES OF AL 'IMRAN.`

segments.voice: Verse 190 says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding. Verse 191 says who they are: those who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth. And what they say, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." Then: glory be to You, protect us from the punishment of the Fire. Three postures cover almost every moment of a human life: work, rest, sleep, sickness. Remembrance isn't tied to one position or one hour. The same three show up in a hadith about prayer. A sick companion asked how to pray, and the Prophet told him: standing; if you can't, then sitting; if you can't, then on your side. Nobody is too weak to be counted. Then the second act: reflection, tafakkur. Not just looking at the stars, but thinking until a conclusion comes out of your mouth: You didn't make this in vain. Batil, the word for in vain, means empty, pointless, false. The people in the verse look at the night sky and conclude the opposite. So the surah that began with clear and ambiguous verses ends here, after the chosen family, Maryam, the rope, Uhud and its grief, and death tasted: a person under the night sky, in whatever posture they can manage, saying: not in vain.
screen: `SIGNS IN NIGHT AND DAY` · `STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN` · `TAFAKKUR: THINKING IT THROUGH` · `BATIL: EMPTY, POINTLESS` · then, large: `THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.`

segments.voice: Choose your posture, stand, sit or lie down, whichever your body wants, and picture the night sky: the dark, the scattered lights, the distances. Let the size of it settle on you until one thought forms slowly, the way it did for the people in the verse: this is not pointless. If you pray, you can say the verse's own words: Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.
Standing. Standing, sitting, and lying down: remembering God in every posture, and reflecting on creation, from 3:191. Today's word.
Your line: not in vain. Any posture will do. That's Al 'Imran, start to finish.

376.title: One soul
376.hook: He created you from a single soul and made its mate, so respect the wombs that bore you (4:1)
376.howItsDone: Muslims hear 4:1 in the khutbat al-hajah, the Prophet's opening sermon recited at many weddings and Friday sermons, and the verse is a basis for keeping ties of kinship, silat al-rahim, a duty stressed throughout Islamic teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the end of Al 'Imran, standing, sitting, lying down, and our Lord, You did not create this in vain. Your line was not in vain.

At a great many Muslim weddings, before the vows, someone stands and gives a short sermon that the Prophet ﷺ used to open important speeches. It quotes three verses. One is the first verse of the fourth surah, an-Nisa, the Women. So as two families are being joined, the room hears a verse about where all families came from. Today, that verse, and a new surah that will spend a long time on family, inheritance and fairness.
screen: `A SERMON BEFORE THE VOWS.` → `AN-NISA, THE WOMEN.` → `WHERE ALL FAMILIES CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: Surah 4 opens by speaking to everyone: O mankind. Then, in Pickthall's words, be careful of your duty to your Lord "Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate." From those two, He spread abroad many men and women. One soul: nafs wahida. Before any nation, tribe, language or family name, a single origin. Every person you'll meet today is, in the verse's picture, a relative. Then a phrase that's easy to pass over: be mindful of God, by whom you ask things of one another, and of the arham. Arham means wombs, and by extension kinship, the ties of family. And here's the detail. Rahim, womb, comes from the same root as rahma, mercy, and ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes the link explicit: the word for womb is taken from the name ar-Rahman, and whoever keeps its ties, God keeps ties with them. So the surah of the Women begins by placing mothers, wombs and family ties right next to God's own mercy. That's why it fits a wedding. Two families joining are reminded they were already one, and what they owe each other. In the coming days an-Nisa gets very specific: orphans, inheritance shares, kindness in marriage, neighbors near and far. It all grows out of this first verse. One soul, many people, ties of mercy between them.
screen: `O MANKIND: SPOKEN TO EVERYONE` · `NAFS WAHIDA: ONE SOUL` · `ARHAM: WOMBS, AND KINSHIP` · `RAHIM AND RAHMA: ONE ROOT` · then, large: `FROM A SINGLE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Think of your mother, or whoever carried and raised you; if she has died, or that relationship is hard, simply hold her in mind for a moment, or think of another woman who mothered you. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for her. Then widen the circle to the people around you today, strangers included, and remember the verse's claim: from one soul.
One soul. Nafs wahida: all people from a single soul and its mate, the opening of an-Nisa, 4:1. Today's word.
Your line: from one soul. In the verse's picture, every stranger is a relative. See you tomorrow.

377.title: The orphans' property
377.hook: give orphans their property and don't swap bad for good (4:2)
377.howItsDone: Muslims treat caring for orphans and guarding their wealth as a serious duty; orphan sponsorship is a widespread form of Muslim charity, and Islamic law sets rules for guardians managing a minor's property.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the opening of an-Nisa, all people from one soul, and the ties of the womb. Your line was from one soul.

A father dies and leaves a flock of good sheep to his young son. An uncle will manage them, and keep the ledger, until the boy grows up. The uncle has a few sickly sheep of his own. Nobody's checking. He could swap a healthy one for a sick one, once, quietly. Or mix the two flocks together, and let the numbers blur. The second verse of an-Nisa sees that guardian, and that ledger, very clearly.
screen: `A GUARDIAN WITH A LEDGER.` → `A HEALTHY SHEEP FOR A SICK ONE.` → `NOBODY'S CHECKING.`

segments.voice: Surah 4, verse 2, says: give orphans their property. Don't exchange the good for the bad. Don't eat up their wealth by mixing it with your own; that is a great sin. Three precise warnings, aimed at exactly the tricks a guardian might use. Some commentators read these lines against Medina after Uhud, with its new orphans and widows. A few verses later, 4:6 gives a whole procedure. Test the orphans as they near the age of marriage. If you find sound judgment in them, rushd, hand their property over. Don't rush to spend it before they grow up. A guardian who is well off should take nothing for his work; a poor one may take what is fair. And when you hand it over, call witnesses. Then 4:10 gives a stark picture: those who unjustly consume orphans' wealth are swallowing fire into their bellies. Why so much care? One reason is close to home. The Prophet ﷺ was himself an orphan. His father died before he was born, and his mother while he was still a small child. Surah 93 says to him, in Pickthall's words: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?" And a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports him holding up two fingers, side by side, and saying that he and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this. The verse turns that warmth into accounting. Love the orphan, yes, and keep the ledger straight, because theirs is theirs.
screen: `NO SWAPPING, NO MIXING` · `TEST FOR SOUND JUDGMENT, THEN HAND IT OVER` · `THE PROPHET WAS AN ORPHAN` · `TWO FINGERS, SIDE BY SIDE` · then, large: `GIVE ORPHANS THEIR PROPERTY.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind a child who has lost a parent, someone you know, a family in your community, or children you'll never meet, without rushing to fix anything. If you pray, you can ask God to protect them, and you might think of one real way to help: a sponsorship, a donation, time with a child who needs an adult.
Yatim, an orphan. Theirs to receive in full, with no swapping, no mixing, handed over with witnesses, from 4:2 to 4:10. Today's word.
Your line: theirs is theirs. The Prophet knew what it was to be an orphan. Day three hundred seventy-seven, done.

378.title: The shares
378.hook: the inheritance verses set shares for daughters, sons, parents, spouses (4:11–12)
378.howItsDone: Muslims divide estates according to the shares in 4:11–12 and 4:176, after debts and any bequest of up to a third; the detailed calculation is a field of Islamic law called 'ilm al-fara'id, and many Muslims write an Islamic will.

segments.voice: Yesterday: yatim, the orphans' property, no swapping, no mixing. Your line was theirs is theirs.

After Uhud, a widow came to the Prophet ﷺ with her two daughters. Their father, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', had been killed in the battle, and their uncle had taken everything Sa'd owned. Commentators describe the old custom: the men who could fight inherited, and women and girls were left out. She asked the Prophet plainly: who will marry these girls with nothing? The reports say the inheritance verses came down soon after.
screen: `A WIDOW AND TWO DAUGHTERS.` → `THE UNCLE TOOK EVERYTHING.` → `WHO WILL CARE FOR THESE GIRLS?`

segments.voice: The word is mirath, inheritance, from a root meaning to inherit, to be left something. Verses 11 and 12 of an-Nisa set fixed shares, by name. Daughters inherit. Mothers inherit. Wives and husbands inherit from each other. Parents each receive a sixth when there are children. A husband receives half of his wife's estate if she has no children, a quarter if she does; a wife receives a quarter, or an eighth. Sisters and brothers have shares in certain cases. And before anything is divided, the verses repeat, any bequest is honored and debts are paid. In the story, the Prophet sent for the uncle and told him to give the daughters two-thirds, the mother an eighth, and keep the rest. People often ask about one rule: a son receives twice the share of a daughter. Classical scholars explain it by duties: in Islamic law, a man must pay the bride's dower and support his wife and family, while a woman's wealth is her own, owed to no one. Some scholars also point out cases where a woman's share equals or exceeds a man's. Muslims today discuss how these rules apply in modern economies, and families and countries handle them in different ways. A hadith in Bukhari adds a limit: a person may leave up to a third by will, and the Prophet said even a third is a lot; better to leave your heirs well off than dependent. So the shares moved a family's money from whoever was strongest to a list where everyone has a place. This week, from the message outliving the messenger to the shares, has been about what we owe each other.
screen: `MIRATH: WHAT IS LEFT TO YOU` · `DAUGHTERS, MOTHERS, WIVES BY NAME` · `DEBTS FIRST, THEN THE SHARES` · `UP TO A THIRD BY WILL` · then, large: `EVERYONE HAS A SHARE.`

segments.voice: Think, calmly and as an act of care, about what you'd leave behind if your time came: what you own, what you owe, who depends on you, whether anything is written down. Just notice which answers you don't know yet.
Mirath. Inheritance: the shares set out in 4:11 and 12 for daughters, sons, parents and spouses, after debts are paid. Today's word.
Your line: everyone has a share. Daughters, mothers and wives are named in it. A week, and a new surah well begun.
